source_document.body:
Mexico has introduced new requirements for commercial trucking companies seeking voluntary federal certification.
The new program places greater emphasis on digital monitoring, vehicle weight compliance and internal operational controls as the country works to strengthen highway safety and regulatory oversight .
The Ministry of Infrastructure, Communications and Transportation (SICT) published the new requirements Thursday, Nov. 19, in Mexico’s Official Gazette of the Federation . The notice took effect Friday, Nov. 20.
The framework establishes procedures for trucking companies to obtain approval under a self-regulation program known as Autorregulación (Permisionario Responsable con el Cumplimiento de la Norma) , or Responsible Permittee for Compliance with the Standard.
The program operates under Mexico’s NOM-012-SCT-2-2017 regulation, which governs maximum vehicle weights and dimensions on federally regulated highways.
Although participation is voluntary, companies seeking certification must demonstrate that they have implemented internal systems capable of ensuring compliance with federal transportation requirements.
The initiative represents a shift toward recognizing carriers that can document their own compliance practices rather than relying exclusively on government inspections.
According to the SICT, the objective is to improve highway safety , reduce operational risks and make vehicle inspection and verification procedures more efficient.
The program applies to federally permitted general freight carriers and private freight transportation operations.
Digital monitoring becomes central to compliance
One of the program’s most significant elements is the emphasis on electronic documentation and internal monitoring systems.
According to an executive guide issued by Mexico’s National Association of Private Transport (ANTP), participating companies must maintain a permanent digital system capable of recording shipment information in real time and making those records available to federal transportation authorities.
Carriers can qualify through two principal compliance mechanisms: using their own weighing equipment to verify cargo weights or implementing standardized loading procedures that consistently meet federal weight and dimension limits.
Companies may also combine both approaches.
The requirements place greater responsibility on carriers to verify that trucks meet applicable limits before entering federal highways.
For larger trucking fleets, this could mean integrating weighing systems, dispatch operations, shipment documentation and compliance reporting into existing fleet management platforms.
For smaller carriers, however, adopting and maintaining the necessary technology and administrative processes could create additional expenses.
The SICT notice also authorizes federal authorities to recognize weighing results generated by carriers’ own scales or by operators demonstrating consistent loading procedures.
How trucking companies can obtain certification
The SICT’s General Directorate of Federal Motor Transport (DGAF) will oversee the approval process through its Executive Directorate of Supervision.
According to the ANTP’s guidance, applicants must complete a five-stage process involving documentation, regulatory review and verification.
Companies must first assemble the required application documents and submit them to the DGAF. The agency then reviews the documentation and conducts an inspection visit before the applicant presents the required guarantee and receives final approval.
Approved carriers will receive official identification for participating vehicles.
The ANTP said certification and the corresponding vehicle identification will remain valid for three years, subject to continued compliance.
Vehicles participating in the program must display their license plate numbers in the prescribed manner and carry an official certification identifier.
Carriers must also maintain updated information concerning their vehicles, operating permits, business addresses and changes to their loading or compliance procedures.
The program’s requirements and application procedures are available through the DGAF’s official self-regulation portal .
Random inspections and penalties remain in place
Despite the program’s emphasis on voluntary compliance, Mexican authorities will retain the ability to inspect participating trucks.
The SICT said inspections may be conducted at fixed weight and dimension verification centers or through electronic monitoring devices deployed by federal authorities.
Carriers that violate applicable weight, dimension or safety requirements remain subject to penalties under Mexico’s federal transportation laws.
According to the ANTP, exceeding weight or dimension limits more than three times within a year, measured from the first violation, can result in revocation of certification.
Other violations of the program’s operating guidelines may also lead to revocation.
What the changes mean for Mexico’s trucking industry
The new framework could have significant implications for Mexico’s commercial trucking industry, particularly as carriers face growing pressure to improve safety, operating efficiency and supply chain visibility.
Companies with established fleet management technology, weighing infrastructure and compliance departments may be better positioned to obtain certification.
Those operators could benefit from greater predictability in vehicle verification processes and potentially fewer administrative delays associated with demonstrating compliance.
Smaller carriers and independent operators, meanwhile, may face greater challenges meeting the program’s digital documentation and procedural requirements.
The framework could also encourage greater investment in fleet management software, electronic shipment records, weighing technology and standardized loading systems.
For shippers, the certification program could provide an additional way to evaluate carriers’ operational controls and commitment to regulatory compliance.
The initiative also comes as Mexico’s trucking industry faces broader challenges involving highway security, operating costs and government enforcement.
Why it matters: Mexico’s transportation ministry’s expanded trucking compliance framework program could accelerate the adoption of digital compliance systems across the country’s trucking industry while creating new operational and administrative demands for carriers.
